text:
A suspension bridge does not make its span primarily by bending a heavy beam, like a girder. Instead, it turns the span into a tension system. The deck, the walking surface carrying traffic, is usually relatively light and flexible. Load from cars, people, snow, and attached structures is spread through the deck, then collected at evenly spaced points where vertical suspender cables attach. Those suspenders are close to vertical, so most of the deck load is carried upward as tension in the suspenders. Think of them as a set of many small ropes holding the road up, rather than as one rigid plank fighting a deep bending moment.

At the top of each suspender, the load enters a pair of main cables, one on each side of the bridge, that run roughly along the length of the span. Those main cables are the heavy tension members. They hang in a sagging curve, like a strand of thick rope or a flattened catenary, passing over saddles on the towers and continuing outward to massive anchorages near or beyond the ends of the span. When suspenders pull down on the main cable between towers, the cable sags until the geometry balances the load. The curve is not arbitrary: a quickly sagging cable needs less horizontal tension to hold a given set of loads steady, while a nearly straight cable must be pulled much harder. That relationship is the heart of suspension. The deck is not holding itself up by rigidity; it is hanging from a pair of curved tension chords, and the shape of the curve is what turns vertical traffic into manageable cable forces.

The main cable is pulled outward toward the anchorage at each end while also being pushed down between towers by suspender loads. Along the cable, the vertical component of tension changes as it passes from near-level behavior near midspan to steeper pulls near the towers and anchorages, while the horizontal component remains a dominant, roughly constant part of the cable’s tension. Near midspan, the cable locally behaves almost like a shallow arch with very little vertical rise; closer to the supports, the cable climbs more steeply and the vertical components become larger. In effect, bending moment in a ordinary bridge is replaced by cable tension plus the shape change of the cable. Every pound on the deck is ultimately reflected in the tension of the main cables, but the cables deliver that force into the towers and anchorages rather than transferring it span-by-span through one thick beam.

Each tower behaves mostly as a vertical compression member, but it is also a frame with meaningful bending. The two cable branches over a tower produce downward force on the saddle, increasing compression in the tower. The lateral tendency of the cables, pulling the whole tension system toward the anchorages, is met by the stiffness and alignment of the tower legs, by any cross-bracing or portal structure, and especially by the foundation’s ability to resist spreading, sliding, and overturning. The towers are therefore usually massive, often pairs of vertical legs tied together, designed as columns that carry large compressive loads without yielding uselessly sideways. Wind and temperature can change the cable shape and the internal forces, so the towers allow some elastic motion rather than forcing the cables to do all the balancing in one rigid posture.

The critical ground-bearing part is not only the towers but also the anchorage zones. At each end, the main cable is transferred to a block of massive concrete or stone that bears against soil or bedrock. This anchorage resists the outward horizontal pull of the cable and the downward vertical component, using gravity, friction, interlock with rock or strong soil, and large bearing areas to avoid being pulled outward. The end abutments and containment walls help keep the anchorage stable and the approach span continuous with the roadway. In some bridges the main cables are passed through the abutments and anchored deep behind them; in others, separate anchorage blocks sit beyond the end supports. In either case, the ground must be able to provide the horizontal reaction needed to keep the cable system from spreading like an overstretched elastic band.

So the load path runs like this: traffic and deck weight move down through the deck to the suspenders; suspender tension rises into the main cables; the main cables curve over the towers and then travel to the anchorages; the towers carry mainly compression, with some bending and overturning, into deep foundations such as piles or drilled shafts bearing on rock or compacted soil; and the anchorage blocks, tied into the ground at the ends, supply the outward-resisting horizontal force and vertical seat needed for the whole tension system. The bridge’s long span depends less on a single strong beam resisting bending than on a carefully shaped system of taut cables that do the work of a very long, very flexible arch.
